```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
}
options(poolinfo.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
# Bounds in the text are rounded outward, so that they stay true.
up <- function(x, digits = 2) num(ceiling(x * 10^digits - 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
sci <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
pct <- function(x) round(100 * x)
has_metafor <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)
```

`reliability_posterior()` reports a posterior mean and a 95% posterior
interval for each diagnostic, and the posterior probability that the
informativeness $I$ exceeds 1/2. In this vignette we explain where these
numbers come from and which choices lie behind them. We start with the model
and its prior, compare a posterior mean with a plug-in value, and explain
the interval for the dispersion $H$. We then come back to the prior for
trials with few sites, and end with posterior draws, for summaries that the
package does not compute. Our examples are the eight schools of @rubin1981
and the passing outcome of the Online Credit Recovery Study [@rickles2024].

```{r library}
library(poolinfo)
```

## The model and the prior

We work with the normal hierarchical model in which site $j$'s estimate
$\hat\tau_j$ has a known sampling variance $v_j$,

$$
\hat\tau_j \mid \tau_j \sim N(\tau_j, v_j), \qquad
\tau_j \sim N(\mu, \sigma_\tau^2), \qquad j = 1, \dots, J,
$$

independently over sites. By default the prior is flat on the mean $\mu$ and
on the between-site standard deviation $\sigma_\tau$. A prior flat on
$\sigma_\tau$ is not flat on the variance. As a density in $\sigma_\tau^2$
it is proportional to $1/\sigma_\tau$, so it puts less weight on large
variances than a flat prior on $\sigma_\tau^2$ would [@gelman2006].
Integrating $\mu$ out leaves a posterior for $\sigma_\tau$ alone, known up
to a constant, and `vignette("implementation")` gives its formula. Every
diagnostic depends only on $\sigma_\tau$ and the $v_j$, so its posterior
mean, its quantiles and the probability that it exceeds a value are
one-dimensional integrals over that posterior. Because the package computes
them by quadrature rather than simulation, they have no Monte Carlo error.

Our first example, `eight_schools`, has the estimated effects of coaching on
the SAT-V in eight schools, with their standard errors. We fit the
posterior.

```{r eight-fit}
schools <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = school,
                                 data = eight_schools,
                                 scale_label = "SAT-V point")
schools
```

```{r eight-facts, include = FALSE}
ps <- profile_summary(schools)
val <- function(q, col = "mean") ps[[col]][ps$quantity == q]
gm_se <- exp(mean(log(eight_schools$se)))
sigma_c <- sqrt(gm_se^2 * 0.5 / (1 - 0.5))
stopifnot(
  val("sigma_tau", "upper") / val("sigma_tau", "lower") > 50,
  val("I", "lower") < 0.005, val("I", "upper") < 0.75,
  max(eight_schools$se) == 18, min(eight_schools$se) == 9,
  abs(prob_above(schools) -
        prob_above(schools, threshold = gm_se, which = "sigma_tau")) < 1e-12,
  abs(sigma_c - gm_se) < 1e-12
)
```

The posterior of $\sigma_\tau$ is wide. Its 95% interval runs from
`r num(val("sigma_tau", "lower"))` to `r num(val("sigma_tau", "upper"), 1)`
SAT-V points, and the interval for $I$ runs from `r num(val("I", "lower"))`
to `r num(val("I", "upper"))`.

In the last block, Pr(I > 0.5)
is the posterior probability that $\sigma_\tau^2$ exceeds $\mathrm{GM}(v)$,
the geometric mean of the sampling variances. The threshold 1/2 is where the
leading term of $\bar S - I$ changes sign [@lee2026, Proposition 2], as
`vignette("poolinfo")` explains.

`plot_sigma_scale()` plots the posterior density of $\sigma_\tau$ with a
second axis for $I$, and shades the region where $I$ exceeds 1/2.

```{r sigma-scale, fig.alt = "The posterior density of sigma_tau for the eight schools, highest at 0 and falling, with a second axis for the informativeness and the region where it exceeds 1/2 shaded."}
plot_sigma_scale(schools)
```

```{r sigma-facts, include = FALSE}
dens_sigma <- functional_density(schools, "sigma_tau")
stopifnot(all(diff(dens_sigma$density) < 0))
if (has_metafor) {
  reml8 <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, data = eight_schools,
                        method = "REML")
  stopifnot(reml8$tau2 < 1e-8)
}
```

The density is highest at 0 and falls steadily. The shading starts at
$\sigma_\tau = \sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)} = `r num(gm_se, 1)`$ points, where
$I = 1/2$, and `r num(prob_above(schools), 3)` of the probability lies
beyond it. Because $I$ increases with $\sigma_\tau$, each quantile of $I$ is
$I$ at the same quantile of $\sigma_\tau$, which the top axis lets you read
off.

## Posterior means and plug-in values

The printed fit gives the posterior mean of $I$ in its first row and, in its
last line, $I$ at the posterior mean of $\sigma_\tau^2$. That is the value
you would get by putting this estimate of $\sigma_\tau^2$ into the formula
for $I$. `plugin_gap()` gives both, and their difference, for four
diagnostics.

```{r gap}
print(plugin_gap(schools), digits = 3)
```

```{r gap-facts, include = FALSE}
gap <- plugin_gap(schools)
q <- schools$quantiles
median_sigma2 <- q$median[q$quantity == "sigma_tau2"]
stopifnot(all(gap$difference > 0), gap$difference[1] > 0.1,
          val("sigma_tau2") > 2 * median_sigma2)
```

For the eight schools the two values of $I$ are far apart,
`r num(gap$posterior_mean[1], 3)` against `r num(gap$at_mean_sigma2[1], 3)`.
The posterior mean averages $I$ over the values of $\sigma_\tau$ that the
data allow. The plug-in value first averages $\sigma_\tau^2$ and then
applies $I$, and the long right tail pulls the posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau^2$, `r num(val("sigma_tau2"), 1)`, far above its median,
`r num(median_sigma2, 1)`. Whatever the data, $I$ is a concave function of
$\sigma_\tau^2$. By Jensen's inequality, then, its posterior mean is at most
its value at the posterior mean of $\sigma_\tau^2$, with equality only when
the posterior of $\sigma_\tau^2$ is a point mass [@lee2026, Proposition 3].
The same holds for every $S_j$, and so for $\bar S$.

Proposition 3 gives no such order for $H$ and $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and the
positive differences in their rows are a property of these data. For the
passing outcome of the credit recovery study, with 32 sites, the difference
for $H$ is negative.

```{r passing-gap}
passing <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = ocrs)
print(plugin_gap(passing), digits = 3)
```

```{r passing-gap-facts, include = FALSE}
gap_passing <- plugin_gap(passing)
stopifnot(all(gap_passing$difference[1:2] > 0),
          gap_passing$difference[3] < 0)
```

Here $I$ and $\bar S$ again come out larger at the posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau^2$, as they must, while $H$ comes out smaller, by
`r sci(-gap_passing$difference[3])`.

A third number is common in practice, $I$ at a point estimate of
$\sigma_\tau^2$ such as the REML estimate. For the eight schools that
estimate is 0, which makes every reliability 0. `reliability_profile()`
computes the profile at any value of $\sigma_\tau$, or at the estimate of a
metafor fit, but such a profile carries no uncertainty about $\sigma_\tau$.

## Intervals

The posterior intervals are central, with 2.5% of the posterior probability
below the lower end and 2.5% above the upper end. We use central intervals
because they carry over through increasing functions. $I$, $\bar S$ and
$J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ increase with $\sigma_\tau$, so the ends of their
intervals are their values at the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of $\sigma_\tau$.
A highest-density interval does not carry over in general, since a nonlinear
change of scale moves the region of highest density. For the eight schools
it would also run from 0, where the density of $\sigma_\tau$ is highest, to
the 95% quantile.

```{r interval-facts, include = FALSE}
gm_v <- gm_se^2
s_lo <- val("sigma_tau", "lower")
s_hi <- val("sigma_tau", "upper")
H_max <- schools$h_branches$H_max
path <- profile_path(schools, n = 20001)
above <- path$sigma_tau[path$H >= val("H", "upper")]
stopifnot(
  abs(val("I", "lower") - s_lo^2 / (s_lo^2 + gm_v)) < 1e-12,
  abs(val("I", "upper") - s_hi^2 / (s_hi^2 + gm_v)) < 1e-12,
  val("H", "upper") < H_max, H_max - val("H", "upper") < 0.01 * H_max,
  abs(prob_above(schools, min(above), "sigma_tau") -
        prob_above(schools, max(above), "sigma_tau") - 0.025) < 0.002
)
```

The dispersion $H$ needs more care. It is 0 at $\sigma_\tau = 0$, peaks
where $\bar S = I$, and returns toward 0 as $\sigma_\tau$ grows, so each
value of $H$ below the peak comes from two values of $\sigma_\tau$. The
package adds the posterior probabilities of the two branches to get the
distribution function of $H$, and solves it for the quantiles. For the eight
schools the interval for $H$ runs from `r num(val("H", "lower"), 5)` to
`r num(val("H", "upper"), 5)`, just below the largest value that $H$ can
take with these standard errors, `r num(H_max, 5)`. The upper end is so
close to the largest value because $H$ is flat near its peak. Every
$\sigma_\tau$ from `r num(min(above), 1)` to `r num(max(above), 1)` points
gives a value of $H$ above the upper end, and these values of $\sigma_\tau$
carry the remaining 2.5% of the probability.

`functional_density()` returns the posterior density of a diagnostic on a
grid, by a change of variables from the density of $\sigma_\tau$, and
`plot_functionals()` plots it with the posterior mean, the plug-in value and
the 95% interval.

```{r density, fig.alt = "The posterior density of the informativeness for the eight schools, unbounded near 0, with the posterior mean as a solid line, the value at the posterior mean of sigma_tau squared as a dashed line and the 95% interval shaded."}
plot_functionals(schools)
```

```{r density-facts, include = FALSE}
dens_I <- functional_density(schools, "I")
priors_all <- list(sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 10),
                   sd_prior("half_t", scale = 10, df = 3),
                   sd_prior("half_cauchy", scale = 5),
                   sd_prior("uniform", upper = 50))
at_zero <- vapply(priors_all, function(p) {
  functional_density(update(schools, prior = p), "sigma_tau")$density[1]
}, 0)
stopifnot(all(diff(dens_I$density) < 0), dens_I$density[1] > 100,
          dens_sigma$density[1] > 0, all(at_zero > 0))
```

The solid line marks the posterior mean of $I$,
`r num(gap$posterior_mean[1], 3)`, the dashed line the plug-in value,
`r num(gap$at_mean_sigma2[1], 3)`, and the shading the interval up to
`r num(val("I", "upper"))`. Near $I = 0$ the density is unbounded, and the
plot cuts its vertical axis. Under the flat prior, as under every prior that
`sd_prior()` offers, the posterior density of $\sigma_\tau$ is positive at
0. Close to 0 the informativeness is nearly $\sigma_\tau^2/\mathrm{GM}(v)$,
so the density of $I$ grows like $I^{-1/2}$ as $I$ approaches 0. A gray line
marks the threshold 1/2.

`prob_above()` computes the posterior probability that $I$, $\bar S$,
$J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ or $\sigma_\tau$ itself exceeds a value. We ask for the
probability that $\sigma_\tau$ exceeds 5 SAT-V points.

```{r prob}
prob_above(schools, threshold = 5, which = "sigma_tau")
```

```{r prob-facts, include = FALSE}
p5 <- prob_above(schools, threshold = 5, which = "sigma_tau")
stopifnot(p5 > 0.5, p5 < 0.55)
```

It is `r num(p5)`, a little over a half.

## Few sites and the prior

With few sites the posterior of $\sigma_\tau$ is wide, and the prior
matters. Under the flat prior, the package's default and the prior of
@lee2026, the
posterior is proper only with at least 3 sites, the posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau$ exists only with at least 4, and that of $\sigma_\tau^2$ only
with at least 5. `?sd_prior` gives these counts for a mean model and for the
other priors. When a posterior mean does not exist, the printed fit reports
it as not defined. We fit the first 4 of the eight schools.

```{r four}
four <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = eight_schools[1:4, ])
four
```

```{r four-facts, include = FALSE}
ps4 <- profile_summary(four)
I4 <- ps4$mean[ps4$quantity == "I"]
sigma4_upper <- ps4$upper[ps4$quantity == "sigma_tau"]
p20_4 <- prob_above(four, threshold = 20, which = "sigma_tau")
p20_8 <- prob_above(schools, threshold = 20, which = "sigma_tau")
proper4 <- update(four, prior = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 10))
proper8 <- update(schools, prior = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 10))
proper_I4 <- proper4$summary$mean[proper4$summary$quantity == "I"]
proper_I8 <- proper8$summary$mean[proper8$summary$quantity == "I"]
stopifnot(I4 > 1.8 * val("I"), sigma4_upper > 80, p20_4 > 5 * p20_8, proper_I4 > proper_I8,
          all(diff(functional_density(four, "sigma_tau")$density) < 0))
if (has_metafor) {
  reml4 <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, data = eight_schools[1:4, ],
                        method = "REML")
  stopifnot(reml4$tau2 < 1e-8)
}
```

The posterior mean of $I$ is now `r num(I4)`, against `r num(val("I"))` with
all 8 schools, and the 95% interval of $\sigma_\tau$ reaches
`r num(sigma4_upper, 0)` points. For both sets the REML estimate of
$\sigma_\tau$ is 0, but four schools say less about $\sigma_\tau$ than
eight. Under the flat prior the posterior density of $\sigma_\tau$ falls
off like $\sigma_\tau^{1-J}$, slowly when $J = 4$, and the posterior
probability that $\sigma_\tau$ exceeds 20 points is `r num(p20_4)` with 4
schools against `r num(p20_8)` with 8. The posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau^2$ does not exist with 4 sites, so the printout has no plug-in
value. Under a half-normal prior with scale 10 the two sets differ as well,
with posterior means of $I$ of `r num(proper_I4)` and `r num(proper_I8)`.

Proper priors on $\sigma_\tau$ are a common alternative when there are few
sites, such as half-normal or half-t priors with a scale on the scale of the
effects [@gelman2006]. `sd_prior()` makes them, and `prior_sensitivity()`
refits a posterior under each and collects the fits:

```{r priors}
prior_sensitivity(schools, list(
  `half-normal, scale 10` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 10),
  `half-t, scale 10, 3 df` = sd_prior("half_t", scale = 10, df = 3),
  `half-Cauchy, scale 5` = sd_prior("half_cauchy", scale = 5)
))
```

```{r prior-facts, include = FALSE}
sens <- as.data.frame(prior_sensitivity(schools, list(
  hn = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 10),
  ht = sd_prior("half_t", scale = 10, df = 3),
  hc = sd_prior("half_cauchy", scale = 5)
)))
stopifnot(all(sens$I[-1] < sens$I[1]), all(sens$I_upper[-1] < sens$I_upper[1]))
```

All three put more weight on small values of $\sigma_\tau$ than the flat
prior does. They pull the posterior mean of $I$ down from `r num(sens$I[1])`
to between `r num(min(sens$I[-1]))` and `r num(max(sens$I[-1]))`, and the
interval's upper end from `r num(sens$I_upper[1])` to between
`r num(min(sens$I_upper[-1]))` and `r num(max(sens$I_upper[-1]))`. We would
name the prior in any report on a trial this small, and show the fits under
more than one.

A given prior matters less as the number of sites grows. To see this with
the trial and the scale of the effects held fixed, we refit the passing
outcome in its 13 Algebra 1 sites, its 19 English 9 sites and all 32 sites,
each under two half-normal priors. A scale of 0.1 is about 0.8 times the
geometric-mean standard error $\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}$ in each set, as the scale 10
is for the eight schools. A scale of 0.5, a between-site standard deviation
of 50 percentage points, is far beyond any plausible spread of effects on
passing, so that prior is weak. For each set we compute how far each prior
moves the posterior mean of $I$ from its value under the flat prior.

```{r sites-and-prior}
half_normal <- list(`scale 0.1` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 0.1),
                    `scale 0.5` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 0.5))
subsets <- list(`Algebra 1` = ocrs[ocrs$subject == "Algebra 1", ],
                `English 9` = ocrs[ocrs$subject == "English 9", ],
                all = ocrs)
shift <- sapply(subsets, function(d) {
  fit <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = d)
  I <- as.data.frame(prior_sensitivity(fit, half_normal))$I
  setNames(I[-1] - I[1], names(half_normal))
})
data.frame(sites = sapply(subsets, nrow), round(t(shift), 3),
           check.names = FALSE)
```

```{r sites-and-prior-facts, include = FALSE}
relative_scale <- sapply(subsets, function(d) 0.1 / exp(mean(log(d$se))))
sd_I <- profile_summary(passing)$sd[1]
stopifnot(
  identical(unname(sapply(subsets, nrow)), c(13L, 19L, 32L)),
  all(relative_scale > 0.7), all(relative_scale < 0.85),
  abs(10 / gm_se - 0.82) < 0.01,
  all(shift < 0), all(diff(abs(shift[1, ])) < 0),
  all(abs(shift[2, ]) < 0.01),
  abs(shift[1, 3]) / sd_I > 0.45, abs(shift[1, 3]) / sd_I < 0.65
)
```

Under the prior with scale 0.1 the posterior mean of $I$ falls by
`r num(-shift[1, 1], 3)` with 13 sites, `r num(-shift[1, 2], 3)` with 19 and
`r num(-shift[1, 3], 3)` with 32. Under the weak prior it falls by
`r up(-min(shift[2, ]), 3)` or less. So a weak prior hardly matters with 32
sites, but a prior with a scale near the standard errors still moves $I$ by
about half of its posterior standard deviation, `r num(sd_I, 3)`.

## Draws

Some summaries need posterior draws, for example those that involve several
site effects at once. `profile_draws()` draws $\sigma_\tau$ by inverting its
posterior distribution function, then the mean given $\sigma_\tau$, and,
with `sites = TRUE`, the site effects given both. With `seed` the draws are
reproducible, and the session's random number generator is left as it was.
We use draws to find the posterior probability that school A, whose estimate
is the largest, also has the largest effect:

```{r draws}
draws <- profile_draws(schools, ndraws = 4000, seed = 1, sites = TRUE)
effects <- draws[, paste0("effect_", eight_schools$school)]
top_A <- mean(apply(effects, 1, which.max) == 1)
round(c(probability = top_A,
        mcse = sqrt(top_A * (1 - top_A) / nrow(draws))), 4)
```

```{r draws-facts, include = FALSE}
best <- table(factor(apply(effects, 1, which.max), levels = 1:8))
mcse_A <- sqrt(top_A * (1 - top_A) / nrow(draws))
stopifnot(which.max(best) == 1, which.max(eight_schools$estimate) == 1,
          top_A > 0.2, top_A < 0.3)
```

School A has the largest effect in `r pct(top_A)`% of the draws, more often
than any other school but far from always, because the model pulls the eight
effects toward one another. The draws are independent, so the Monte Carlo
standard error of this proportion is the binomial one, `r num(mcse_A, 3)`.
Four times as many draws would halve it.

Draws from other software go to `reliability_draws()`, which computes the
diagnostics at each draw of $\sigma_\tau$ and reports their Monte Carlo
standard errors. It reads a brms fit of this model directly, and
`vignette("implementation")` has an example.

## Integration checks

The numerical integration is checked as each fit is made, and
`check_numerics()` shows the results. If a check falls outside its limit,
`reliability_posterior()` warns as it builds the fit.
`vignette("implementation")` explains the checks and the other method of
integration, `posterior_control(engine = "adaptive")`.
